card.name: Maringa
card.tagline: Bakongo couple-dance that grew into Congolese rumba
card.profile: Maringa was a Bakongo partnered couple-dance and music style of the former Kingdom of Loango (spanning today's Republic of the Congo, southern Gabon and Angola's Cabinda) that flourished in the bar-dancing culture of Brazzaville and Leopoldville in the 1920s-1940s. According to Wikipedia's 'Music of the Democratic Republic of the Congo', early maringa used a likembe (lamellophone), a glass bottle struck as a triangle and the patenge frame drum, with dancers swaying the hips and shifting weight from leg to leg; per Wikipedia's 'Congolese rumba', imported Cuban son records transformed maringa into Congolese rumba during the mid-1940s and 1950s.
card.insight: Maringa is the direct ancestor of Congolese rumba - which UNESCO inscribed in 2021 (16.COM, decided 14 December 2021) - making it a foundational root of soukous, ndombolo and much of modern African popular dance (Wikipedia; UNESCO).
card.image_significance: The hip-sway that became rumba. A representative image shows drum-driven communal movement, often in a circle with vivid textiles — Lower Congo (Bakongo), Congo/Angola.
